narrative:
The model estimated a 60.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success, so your law school application was rejected. This is a prediction based on patterns in past students, not a verdict about your ability.

The denial was driven most strongly by your upper-middle family income bracket, which was the top influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Your third-year class rank was the second most important factor and pushed the other way: you are in the top decile (10), well above the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, which is a clear sign of academic strength. The third most important factor was your LSAT score of 45, which also pushed the prediction toward failure in this assessment.

Because the strongest factor was income—something you cannot change—treat this as a model-based risk flag rather than a complete judgment. Ask for an individual review and submit evidence that addresses exam readiness: your strong third-year rank, any upward grade trend, and a concrete bar-preparation plan. Consider retaking the LSAT if feasible, seek admissions advising, and ask whether delayed entry or conditional acceptance with added support is available. Gender and race were not used in this decision.
